## Exercises 17.2.5 {.unnumbered}

### Question 1

> What happens if you parse a string that contains invalid dates?

```{r, eval=FALSE}
ymd(c("2010-10-10", "bananas"))
```

**Solution:**

> It simply fails to parse/transform it into a valid date (here it recognize the first element and raise an error at the second)

### Question 2

> What does the tzone argument to today() do? Why is it important?

**Solution:**

> `tzone` is a character vector specifying which time zone you would like the current time in. tzone defaults to your computer's system timezone.

### Question 3

> For each of the following date-times, show how you’d parse it using a readr column specification and a lubridate function.

```{r}
d1 <- "January 1, 2010"
d2 <- "2015-Mar-07"
d3 <- "06-Jun-2017"
d4 <- c("August 19 (2015)", "July 1 (2015)")
d5 <- "12/30/14" # Dec 30, 2014
t1 <- "1705"
t2 <- "11:15:10.12 PM"
```

**Solution:**

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#d1
mdy(d1)

#d2
ymd(d2)

#d3
dmy(d3)

#d4
mdy(d4)

#d5
mdy(d5)

#t2
# November day 15, 2010, 12 PM (noon)
csv <- "
  date
  11:15:10.12 PM
"
read_csv(csv, col_types = cols(date = col_datetime("%m:%d:%y%.%I%.%p")))

#t1
# Simply 5 PM (17h) & 5 minutes
csv_2 <- "
  time
  1705
"
read_csv(csv_2, col_types = cols(time = col_time("%H%M")))

```

## Exercises 17.3.4 {.unnumbered}

### Question 1

> How does the distribution of flight times within a day change over the course of the year?

**Solution:**

> As you may notice, flight departure times follow a consistent pattern throughout the day, regardless of the month. This pattern likely arises from a strict, standardized flight schedule over the year.

> You might notice the `months in the legend` are written in `French`. This is because lubridate automatically adapts its text outputs to match the system language of the computer running the code. I am `Moroccan`, and we traditionally `study and work in French` (our primary foreign language). However, our universities are slowly but firmly shifting their research to English to `democratize` the language in this context and build a stronger international presence.

```{r}
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
library(ggplot2)

make_datetime_100 <- function(year, month, day, time) {
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100)
}

flights_dt <- flights |> 
  filter(!is.na(dep_time)) |> 
  mutate(
    dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time), 
    dep_hour = floor_date(dep_time, "day")
    ) |> 
  relocate(dep_time, dep_hour)

flights_dt |> 
  mutate(
    # Force every flight to happen on Jan 1st so they all align on one 24-hour x-axis
    time_of_day = update(dep_time, yday = 1),
    # Extract the month to use for color comparison
    month = month(dep_time, label = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time_of_day, color = month)) +
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 3600) + # 3600 seconds = exactly 1 hour bins
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M")
```

### Question 2

> Compare `dep_time`, `sched_dep_time` and `dep_delay`. Are they consistent? Explain your findings.

**Solution:**

```{r}
flights_dt <- flights |> 
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(sched_dep_time), !is.na(dep_delay)) |> 
  mutate(
    dep_time             = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time),
    sched_dep_time       = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_dep_time), 
    actual_delay         = as.numeric((dep_time - sched_dep_time)/60) # delay in minutes
  ) |> 
  select(month, origin, dest, sched_dep_time, dep_time, dep_delay, actual_delay) |> 
  # we keep unique pairs of values because plotting more than 300 000
  # observation is resource-heavy
  count(dep_delay, actual_delay) 

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = flights_dt, aes(x = actual_delay, y = dep_delay), size = 2)+
  geom_abline(colour = 'green', linewidth = 1)+
  geom_abline(intercept = 1440, slope = 1, colour = 'violet', linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    geom = "segment",
    x = -70, y = 0, xend = -1370, yend = 0, color = "red",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed",ends = "both", angle = 10)
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label", x = -850, y = 100,
    label = "24 hours",
    hjust = "left", color = "red"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
  
```

> After inspecting the data, it seems that almost all recorded departure delays are exactly the actual departure delays. The plot, confirms this thanks to the identity line in green (remember we are plotting more then 300 000 recorded flight observations so it is hard to distinguish between the number of points that are on the green line and the rest of it: a simple filter with a condition such as `dep_delay != actual_delay` would inform you about this).

> The other points that are not on the `green line` (`dep_delay` is different than `actual_delay`) indicate that there were flights that departed early (very early actually) but recorded as they were delayed. Suprisingly and bizzarly, they follow a line (actually as if we just moved the identity line to the left and kept the slope i.e the points plotted on the left were supposed to be on the green line but displaced). Remember that this data comes with `dep_delay` and we are the ones that calculates with `mutate` the new variable `actual_delay`. `Here is an interesting catch : let's plot a line with the same slope (1) as the identity line and move it back by 24 hours`(`1440 minutes`). we will come back to this special line as a conclusion about those unresonable data.

> Look at the data below : there are flights that are supposed to depart 2, January at 23:59:00 but departed the same day at 00:42:00 with a departure delay of 43 minutes. It doesn't make any sense, right ? well let's suppose that such data are typing error or some miss-regulated automatic programs and that flight is actually was supposed to depart the same hour but the day befour : now it makes completly sense. The image shows a potential pattern that may happen at the very end of every month. Such a supposition is confirmed with the line in violet above.

![suspicious recorded data](images/data%20inspection.png){width="92%"}

### Question 3 

> Compare `air_time` with the duration between the departure and arrival. Explain your findings. (Hint: consider the location of the airport.)

**Solution:**

> it is impossible for a plane to spend more time in the air than the total time between departure and arrival. The discrepancy you are seeing isn't a problem with the planes; it is a problem with the clocks.

> The Time Zone Trap : In the flights dataset, all departures happen in New York, meaning `dep_time` is always recorded in Eastern Time (EST). However, `arr_time` is recorded in the local time of the destination airport. That's way some data points are plotted below the green identity line.

```{r}
flights_dt <- flights |> 
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |> 
  mutate(
    dep_time        = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time),
    arr_time        = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, arr_time), 
    flight_duration = as.numeric(arr_time - dep_time)
  ) |> 
  # The difference may be negative due to flights that depart most likely at night and arrive 
  # after midnight the day after
  filter(flight_duration >= 0) |> 
  select(dep_time, arr_time, flight_duration, air_time) |> 
  count(flight_duration, air_time)

flights_dt

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = flights_dt, aes(x = air_time, y = flight_duration), size = 2)+
  geom_abline(colour = 'green', linewidth = 1)
```

#### Question 4 

> How does the average delay time change over the course of a day? Should you use `dep_time` or `sched_dep_time`? Why?

**Solution:**

> If we map our delays against the actual dep_time, the x-axis will be misleading. Imagine a massive storm delays all 8:00 PM flights by four hours. They actually take off at midnight. If you group by `dep_time`, your plot will show that midnight has terrible average delays, and 8:00 PM looks perfectly fine.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7

# left plot using sched_dep_tim
flights |> 
  mutate(sched_dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_dep_time), 
         sched_dep_time = floor_date(sched_dep_time, "15 mins"), 
         time_chunk     = update(sched_dep_time, yday = 1)) |> 
  group_by(time_chunk) |> 
  summarize(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time_chunk, y = avg_delay)) +
  geom_line(color = 'steelblue', linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M")+
  labs(title = "Average delay across the day", x = "Time - scheduled depart time", y = "Delay") +
  theme_minimal()


# right plot using dep_time
flights |> 
  mutate(dep_time   = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, dep_time), 
         dep_time   = floor_date(dep_time, "15 mins"), 
         time_chunk = update(dep_time, yday = 1)) |> 
  group_by(time_chunk) |> 
  summarize(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time_chunk, y = avg_delay)) +
  geom_line(color = 'steelblue', linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M")+
  labs(title = "Average delay across the day", x = "Time - depart time", y = "Delay")+
  theme_minimal()

```


### Question 5 

> On what day of the week should you leave if you want to minimise the chance of a delay?

**Solution:**

> As you can see, saturday is the best day to book a flight to minimze your chance of getting delayed.

```{r}
flights |> 
  mutate(sched_dep_time = make_datetime_100(year, month, day, sched_dep_time),
         day_of_week    = wday(sched_dep_time, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
         ) |> 
  group_by(day_of_week) |> 
  summarize(avg_delay =  mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(x = day_of_week, y = avg_delay), fill = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal()
```
### Question 6 

> What makes the distribution of diamonds$carat and flights$sched_dep_time similar?

**Solution:**

> the overall shapes of the curves are completely different. But both datasets share a human behavioral phenomenon called "heaping," which is the tendency for data to cluster heavily around "nice, round numbers." (human beings prefer clean, memorable schedules and measures)

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7

ggplot(data = flights)+
  geom_density(aes(x = sched_dep_time))

ggplot(data = diamonds)+
  geom_density(aes(x = carat))
```
> To go a step further and mathematically prove the "human heaping" concept, you can isolate just the minute portion of the scheduled departures using the modulo operator `%%`. As you can see below, scheduled depar time at regular minutes dominate the top of the list.

```{r}
flights |> 
  mutate(minute = sched_dep_time %% 100) |> 
  count(minute, sort = TRUE) |> 
  head(10)
```

### Question 7 

> Confirm our hypothesis that the early departures of flights in minutes 20-30 and 50-60 are caused by scheduled flights that leave early. Hint: create a binary variable that tells you whether or not a flight was delayed.

**Solution:**

```{r}
flights |> 
  mutate(
    # Extract just the minute from the scheduled departure time (0 to 59)
    sched_minute = sched_dep_time %% 100,
    # Create the binary variable: TRUE if the flight left early, FALSE otherwise
    left_early = dep_delay < 0
  ) |> 
  # Group by the 60 distinct minutes in an hour
  group_by(sched_minute) |> 
  # Calculate the proportion of flights that left early for each minute
  summarize(prop_early = mean(left_early, na.rm = TRUE), 
            n = n()) |> 
  # Plot the results
  ggplot(aes(x = sched_minute, y = prop_early)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 10))
```
## Exercises 17.4.4  {.unnumbered}

### Question 1

> Explain `days(!overnight)` and `days(overnight)` to someone who has just started learning R. What is the key fact you need to know?

**Solution:**

> Well the new variable overnight is a logical vector that contains either `TRUE` (arr_time < dep_time: a flight departed in the night and arrived the day after; after midnight) or `FALSE`. so days(overnight) either add 1 day (days(TRUE))  to the arrival time or leave the arrival time intact by adding 0 (days(FALSE)) to it.


### Question 2 

> Create a vector of dates giving the first day of every month in 2015. Create a vector of dates giving the first day of every month in the current year.

**Solution:**

> You find below,n respectively the code that generate every day of month of the year 2015 and current one

```{r}
datetime_1  <- ymd("2015-01-01")
my_vector_1 <- as.Date(character())

for (mois in 1:12) {
  month(datetime_1) <- mois
  my_vector_1 <- c(my_vector_1, datetime_1)
}

my_vector_1

```


```{r}
datetime_2 <- mdy(paste0("01-01-", as.character(year(today()))))
my_vector_2 <- as.Date(character())

for (mois in 1:12) {
  month(datetime_2) <- mois
  my_vector_2 <- c(my_vector_2, datetime_2)
}

my_vector_2

```

### Question 3 

> Write a function that given your birthday (as a date), returns how old you are in years.

**Solution:**

```{r}
h_age <- today() - ymd("1979-10-14")
h_age

get_age <- function(birthday) {
  birthday <- as_date(birthday)
  (birthday %--% today()) %/% years(1)
}

# Age of Nawfal
get_age("1998-01-10")
```
